READING

**The bank constraint is the load-bearing fact**

The bank's letter of 2026-06-22 is unambiguous: a licence term shorter than the 2039 loan maturity puts the facility under review. PENNYQUAY produces a renewal filed with a dated undertaking. The Board has dealt with exactly this situation twice in the last two years — Cadgarth (2024) and Nant Elwy (2025) — and in both cases the outcome was a six-year term, not fifteen. Six years from 2028 means the licence lapses in 2034, five years before the loan matures. PENNYQUAY therefore almost certainly triggers the bank's own stated threshold. For a two-person scheme carrying GBP 480,000 of debt, a facility placed under review is not a nuisance; it is a potential wound to the scheme's going-concern status. The GBP 8,436 outage saving looks very different once that risk is priced in.

**Does LINTHAUGH avoid the bank problem?**

Yes, if the derogation is granted. A complete renewal file — bearing the actual compliance certificate, not an undertaking — is what earns a fifteen-year term. Fifteen years from 2028 runs to 2043, which clears the loan by four years with room to spare. So LINTHAUGH, if it works, solves the bank problem cleanly. The question is what probability to attach to "if it works."

**Re-reading the Board's refusal pattern**

The raw grant rate in 2025 was 4/11, about 36%. Taken alone that is not reassuring. But the problem statement adds a piece of information that substantially changes the picture: every published refusal named the applicant's failure to show a dated regulatory driver. That is not merely one factor among many — it appears to be the single stated reason across all seven refusals. Blaenclydach is not in that group. The scheme has a hard chain of dated obligations: licence expiry 2028-05-31, renewal deadline 2027-05-31, certificate required for a complete file, 2011 screen incapable of earning one, permitted works window closed until July (after the renewal deadline), no route to the certificate except derogation or falling back to the undertaking. That chain is exactly what the Board says it is looking for. The realistic probability of grant is materially higher than 36% — perhaps two-thirds or better, given that the explicit disqualifying condition is absent.

**Mapping the costs**

LINTHAUGH if granted: GBP 9,000 application + GBP 46,000 deposit + GBP 19,152 lost winter export = GBP 74,152. The deposit is committed on 2026-12-01 before the answer is known on 2027-01-25, so GBP 55,000 is at risk for five weeks. That is the sharpest discomfort of the course.

LINTHAUGH if refused: the GBP 55,000 is gone; eighteen weeks remain to lodge via undertaking (refusal on 2027-01-25, deadline 2027-05-31 — roughly eighteen weeks — is consistent with the problem statement's own arithmetic). The fallback undertaking then costs the July outage of GBP 8,436 plus the Vossbeck July slot confirmation by 2027-04-30. Total in the worst case: GBP 9,000 + GBP 46,000 + GBP 8,436 = GBP 63,436, still with the bank risk from a six-year term.

PENNYQUAY: GBP 8,436 outage, no deposit, but near-certain six-year term and the bank consequence that flows from it.

**The asymmetry**

If PENNYQUAY were merely cheaper while producing the same renewal term, it would be worth serious weight. But it does not produce the same term. It produces a six-year term with two precedents behind it, and the bank has already said what it will do with that outcome. The direct-cost saving of roughly GBP 65,000 (relative to LINTHAUGH's success scenario) is real but second-order against an existential threat to the loan facility.

LINTHAUGH's main downside — the GBP 46,000 non-returnable deposit — is painful but bounded. A loan facility placed under review is not bounded in the same way.

**The fallback availability**

The problem statement says explicitly that a refusal on 2027-01-25 "leaves eighteen weeks to lodge the renewal another way." Rhoswen therefore does not face a binary choice where a refused derogation destroys the renewal entirely. The undertaking route is available as a fallback regardless. LINTHAUGH is a call option on the fifteen-year term, with the undertaking route as the floor. PENNYQUAY goes straight to that floor without trying for the option.

**Why not BALANCED?**

The two courses would be genuinely even if the derogation probability were close to zero, or if the bank risk were genuinely manageable. Neither is true. The dated-driver criterion removes the stated reason for every 2025 refusal, giving the application a qualitatively better profile than the rejected eleven. And the bank has already put its position on paper. These two facts, taken together, tip the scales clearly toward LINTHAUGH.

---

READING
Blaenclydach holds a concrete dated regulatory chain — licence expiry 2028-05-31, renewal deadline 2027-05-31, certificate required, 2011 screen incapable of earning one, permitted window closed until July — that removes the single stated reason behind every 2025 Rivers Board refusal, raising the derogation's grant probability well above the 36% base rate. PENNYQUAY, by contrast, reliably produces a six-year renewal (Cadgarth 2024, Nant Elwy 2025 both confirmed this), which falls five years short of the 2039 loan and triggers the bank's stated review threshold. The direct-cost advantage of PENNYQUAY (GBP 8,436 vs GBP 74,152) is real but second-order against the potential threat to a GBP 480,000 facility; and even in LINTHAUGH's worst case (refusal, GBP 55,000 sunk), the undertaking fallback remains available within the deadline. The deposit risk is bounded; a loan facility placed under review is not.

CALL
LINTHAUGH

GROUNDS
PENNYQUAY's near-certain six-year renewal term, anchored by two direct precedents, falls short of the 2039 loan maturity and triggers the bank's own stated review condition, whereas LINTHAUGH — supported by a dated regulatory driver that eliminates the published reason for every 2025 refusal — is the only realistic path to the fifteen-year term that keeps the facility out of review, and even a refusal leaves the undertaking route intact within the deadline.
